definitions.explanation: A form of Japanese collaborative poetry where two or more poets take turns composing alternating verses of 5-7-5 and 7-7 syllables, building on each other's themes and imagery. Flourished from the Kamakura through Edo periods.

examples.japanese: {連歌|れんが}は{複数|ふくすう}の{歌人|かじん}が{詠|よ}む。
examples.english: Linked verse is composed by multiple poets.

examples.japanese: {室町時代|むろまちじだい}に{連歌|れんが}は{最|もっと}も{盛|さか}んだった。
examples.english: Linked verse was most popular during the Muromachi period.

examples.japanese: {連歌|れんが}は{参加者|さんかしゃ}が{交代|こうたい}で{句|く}を{詠|よ}み、{前|まえ}の{句|く}との{関連|かんれん}を{保|たも}ちながら{展開|てんかい}していく。
examples.english: In linked verse, participants take turns composing stanzas, developing the poem while maintaining a connection to the previous verse.

notes:
CULTURE:
Linked verse originated from the upper and lower halves of the {和歌|わか} (waka) being composed by different people. Major practitioners include {宗祇|そうぎ} (Sōgi) in the Muromachi period. The more informal, humorous variant {俳諧|はいかい}{連歌|れんが} eventually gave rise to {俳句|はいく} (haiku) through the work of {松尾芭蕉|まつおばしょう}.

COMMON COLLOCATIONS:
- {連歌|れんが}を{詠|よ}む (to compose linked verse)
- {連歌|れんが}の{会|かい} (a linked verse gathering)
- {連歌|れんが}{師|し} (linked verse master)

SIMILAR WORDS:
- {俳句|はいく}: haiku — a standalone 5-7-5 verse, descended from the opening verse of {連歌|れんが}
- {和歌|わか}: waka — a 5-7-5-7-7 verse composed by a single poet
